doc.title: Operations on Octet Sequences
doc.para:
Operations on Octet Sequences In TJS2, an octet sequence is pseudo-treated as an object of the Octet class, but an Octet class does not actually exist, nor is it truly an object of an Octet class (however, using the typeof operator on an octet sequence returns "Octet"). However, by treating an octet sequence as an object, several methods and properties become available.
The implementation regarding octet sequences is incomplete.

length The length property returns the length of the octet sequence. Please note that it is a property, not a method. However, values cannot be assigned to this property.
var oct = <% 11 22 33 %>; var n = oct.length; // 3 is assigned to n var n = <% 11 22 33 %>.length; // This also assigns 3

'Numerical' Property By indirectly specifying a number as a property, you can access the octet at that position. The result is represented as a numerical value of the octet. For example, assuming oct is an expression representing an octet sequence, oct[0] will be a number representing the value of the first octet. If the number specifies a position longer than the octet sequence or is negative, an exception will occur.
Assignment expressions cannot be generated.
var oct = <% 11 22 33 44 55 %>; var c = oct[0]; // 0x11 is assigned to c var c = oct[2]; // 0x22 is assigned to c oct[3] = 'A'; // Error because assignment expressions cannot be generated var c = oct[100]; // Error because the value is out of range

unpack The unpack method converts binary data (Octet) into an array (Array) according to the format string specified in the argument and returns it. The specified format string is called a template. A template is a series of type specifier characters and their lengths. When * is specified as the length, it represents all remaining length. If the length is omitted, it is treated as 1.
Syntax : unpack(template string)
The following characters can be used in the template string. a : ASCII string (null-padded) A : ASCII string (space-padded) b : Binary string (low bit to high bit order) B : Binary string (high bit to low bit order) c : Signed 1-byte integer (-128 to 127) C : Unsigned 1-byte integer (0 to 255) d : Double-precision floating point value f : Single-precision floating point value h : Hexadecimal string (low nybble first) H : Hexadecimal string (high nybble first) i : Signed int value (usually 4 bytes) I : Unsigned int value (usually 4 bytes) l : Signed long value (usually 4 bytes) L : Unsigned long value (usually 4 bytes) n : Unsigned short value (network byte order) N : Unsigned long value (network byte order) s : Signed short value (usually 2 bytes) S : Unsigned short value (usually 2 bytes) v : Unsigned short value (little endian) V : Unsigned long value (little endian) x : Skip 1 byte X : Backtrack 1 byte @ : Move to specified position m : Base64 encode
var array = octet.unpack("a4i2");
In this example, the first 4 bytes of octet are treated as ASCII characters, and a 4-character string is output to index 0 of the array. Next, 8 bytes are treated as two 32-bit signed integers and output to index 1 and index 2 of the array. In other words, a string such as "xxxx" is output to array[0], and integers are output to array[1] and array[2].
